cur: For many LGBTQIA+ teenagers, finding a sense of belonging and acceptance can be a difficult and isolating experience. The lack of access to affirming environments in their homes and local communities often leads to severe mental health consequences including an increase risk of suicide.
new: For many LGBTQIA+ teenagers, finding a sense of belonging and acceptance can be a difficult and isolating experience. The lack of affirming environments at home and in their communities is linked to a higher risk of suicide.
tactic: cs-t03 Qualify the scope, keep the commitment
why: The Trevor Project figures in the next block are odds: affirming spaces go with lower risk. Often leads to claims a cause the data does not show, and a hiring manager who reads the cards next will notice the gap. Linked to says exactly what the data says. Also fixes the typo an increase risk, and drops severe mental health consequences, which no data on the page covers (the cards are about suicide attempts only); that also makes room for the new hero line.
src: Data cards: 35% lower odds, 40% less likely (The Trevor Project). CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: This project was developed as part of a UX bootcamp. The brief was to create a functional product for a specific user group and include a way to connect users with an expert.
new: This project was developed as part of a UX bootcamp. The brief was to create a functional product for a specific user group and include a way to connect users with an expert, which Haven calls a Confidante. If a disapproving guardian or peer found Haven on a user’s phone, it could out them, so privacy drives many of the decisions that follow.
tactic: cs-t06 Answer first, with cs-t17 the nut graf and cs-t38 the curse of knowledge
why: The first screen says what Haven is for but not what made it hard, and the constraint that drives the page (being found out) waits until Demographic access. One sentence names it on the first screen, and every privacy decision below pays it off. It also says once what a Confidante is: the word is used in Usability testing before the page explains it.
src: Insight 5 (guardians or peers may find out), Demographic access headline (would out the teens). Confidante as the expert: the brief line plus The Confidante program. CONFIRMED on the page. Many, not every: matching decisions (quiz, profile, flow) are not privacy decisions.

cur: less suicide attempts.
new: lower odds of a suicide attempt.
tactic: cs-t44 Metric theatre (a real number dressed as a different measure)
why: The big 35% reads as 35 percent fewer suicide attempts, but the study measured odds of reporting an attempt, as the card body says. The caption should say what the number is. Also fixes less to the grammatical form.
src: Card 1 body: 35% lower odds of reporting a suicide attempt. CONFIRMED on the page.

field: Links intro (also in Where things stand)
cur: Learn more about what you can do to support LGBTQIA + youth at the links below:
new: Learn more about what you can do to support LGBTQIA+ youth at the links below:
why: LGBTQIA + has a stray space; everywhere else the page writes LGBTQIA+. The line appears twice, so the fix goes in both places.
src: No new claim.

cur: When choosing between experts they value elements that humanize them. Users want to know that experts will understand them.
new: When choosing between experts, users look for what makes each one feel human. They want to know the expert will understand them.
why: They comes before the reader knows who they is, and elements that humanize them is stiff. Users becomes the subject from the first word. This card is tagged on three solution blocks, so it is read more than once.
src: Paraphrase of the card itself. No new claim.

cur: Users need to choose a time when they could be alone. A time that they will feel safe to engage with an expert.
new: Users need to pick a time when they can be alone and feel safe talking to an expert.
why: The second sentence is a fragment and the tenses shift (need, could, will). One sentence says the same thing.
src: Paraphrase of the card itself. No new claim.

cur: Because of the complicated and sensitive nature of the subject matter, I broke this down as if I were designing it as an MVP.
new: Because the subject is complicated and sensitive, I planned Haven as an MVP in two phases: identity first, then community.
tactic: cs-t06 Answer first, with cs-t45 Erudite vernacular
why: The headline hedges (as if I were designing it as an MVP) and leaves the decision, two phases, to the body, which then says broke twice. The new headline states the plan and its order in one line; the chart below it shows the same order.
src: MVP chart: Phase 1 Identity, Phase 2 Community. CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: I broke the design into two phases. This let me decide which features mattered most now and which could wait until after the MVP.
new: Identity comes first because Haven matches each user with a Confidante through who they are. The two phases let me decide which features mattered most now and which could wait until after the MVP.
why: A reviewer will ask why identity comes before community; the research note on Haven calls it the part reviewers probe, and the page never says. The page does show that matching runs on identity (the quiz, ending card 1) and that community suggestions come from the quiz summary. The first sentence states that as the reason. Needs your yes: the reason is my reading of the page, not something you wrote down. If you reject it but accept the headline, the old first sentence repeats the headline and should go.
src: ASSUMED: the reason. Matching on identity CONFIRMED (Primary identity quiz body, Where things stand card 1). research_notes/What gets designers interviewed/haven_through_reviewer_eyes.md, MVP row.

cur: With that all settled, it was time to start building the product. I started designing wireframes to test some of the concepts I had designed based on previous insights.
new: My first wireframes gave users a chat length to pick, a passcode as their only security and top matches to swipe through. Testing changed all three.
tactic: cs-t18 Chekhov’s rifle, with cs-t14 clues before the reveal
why: The current headline is process narration (time to start building) and says nothing a reader can check. The wireframes hold three ideas that testing later changed: the chat length picker, the passcode only security and swiping through matches. Naming them here plants all three, so Scheduling, Confidante profile and Security features each pay one off.
src: Wireframe alts (15 to 60 minute duration, passcode only, top three matches swiped up and down). Changes: Scheduling body (30 minutes), Confidante profile body (replaced vertical swiping), Security screens (PIN with Face ID, the disguise setup). CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: Six participants tested the key flows
new: Six participants tested three key flows.
tactic: re-t38 The oddly precise number (a count that matches the list)
why: Three tasks are listed right under it, so the headline can say three. It is also the only headline without a full stop.
src: Tasks 01 to 03. CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: Users were unsure of what mode of communication they would be chatting with the expert through.
new: Users weren’t sure how they would be talking to the expert.
why: Mode of communication is the stiff version of how they would talk. The insight is tagged on Scheduling a chat, so it is read again there.
src: Paraphrase of the card itself. No new claim.

cur: Users wanted to know more about the Confidante in order to determine the right choice.
new: Users wanted to know more about each Confidante before choosing one.
why: In order to determine the right choice is filler for before choosing one.
src: Paraphrase of the card itself. No new claim.

cur: Based on that feedback and information I had already gathered from initial interviews, I built the following solutions.
new: Each solution below is tagged with the interview and testing insights that shaped it.
tactic: cs-t08 Cite the record, with cs-t38 the curse of knowledge
why: The bridge is the biggest type on the page and says only that solutions follow, a table of contents (cs-t17’s failure). What a cold reader does need is how to read the tags on every solution block (Interview insight 1, Testing insight 4): they are the page’s evidence trail and nothing explains them. One line does.
src: The tags on every solution block. CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: An expert program designed for flexibility, adapting to each user’s unique needs and comfort.
new: The Confidante program is built to adapt to each user’s needs and comfort.
why: A fragment with an -ing tail; it reads generated. A plain sentence with a subject says the same thing. The hero now says what a Confidante is, so this block can stay on how the program adapts.
src: Paraphrase of the headline. No new claim.

cur: Identity shapes what safe, relevant support looks like. The quiz makes room for the experiences behind each match.
new: One identity model for every user would flatten the differences that shape their experience, so the quiz matches users on the experiences they pick.
why: The headline makes a claim without the choice behind it. Insight 3, tagged on this block, names the option that lost: one identity model for everyone. Saying why it lost makes the quiz a decision instead of a feature.
src: Interview insight 3 (one size fits all identity model could flatten differences). Quiz body (users pick experiences; matches built on shared experiences). CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: The quiz groups prompts into five areas: attraction, gender identity, race and ethnicity, belonging and upbringing. Users pick the experiences that matter to them. Confidantes then see a summary of the shared experiences behind each match, so they can tailor support and recommend communities that fit.
new: The quiz groups prompts into five areas: attraction, gender identity, race and ethnicity, belonging and upbringing. Confidantes then see a summary of the shared experiences behind each match, so they can tailor support and recommend communities that fit.
why: With the new headline, Users pick the experiences that matter to them says it a second time. Only if you accept the headline.
src: A cut. No new claim.

cur: Haven’s early flow asked people to choose a Confidante before they could have an introductory chat.
new: Haven’s early flow asked users to choose a Confidante before they could have an introductory chat.
also: In the revised flow, people can chat with more than one Confidante before choosing one.
In the revised flow, users can chat with more than one Confidante before choosing one.
why: People in place of users, twice in the block that matters most. Word swaps only.
src: No new claim.

cur: People needed to know what to expect before booking an introductory chat.
new: Users needed to know what to expect before booking an introductory chat.
why: People in place of users. One word.
src: No new claim.

cur: Testing showed confusion about how chats would work. The scheduling screen explains that they happen by text, last 30 minutes and can end early, so people can choose a private time. With selection moved after the chats, users can book introductions with different Confidantes. Your events lists each upcoming chat with the Confidante’s name and time.
new: Testing showed confusion about how chats would work and how long they would last. The scheduling screen now explains that they happen by text, last a set 30 minutes and can end early, so users can pick a time when they can be alone. Your events lists each upcoming chat with the Confidante’s name and time.
tactic: cs-t48 The rationale recital (a repeat cut), with cs-t18 Chekhov’s rifle paid off
why: With selection moved after the chats repeats the Testing synthesis block one screen up. Cut it. Testing insight 2 (the duration section confused users) is tagged here but the body never answers it; a set 30 minutes does, and it pays off the wireframe’s chat length picker. People becomes users, and a private time becomes Insight 4’s own words (a time when they can be alone).
src: Testing insight 2, Interview insight 4 (tags on this block). Wireframe 1 alt (15 to 60 minute options). Last 30 minutes: this body. CONFIRMED on the page; set is my word for a single length.

cur: The final concept uses text-based sessions, not voice or video, so users can engage without speaking sensitive information aloud. A bounded chat format gives users more control over when and how much they share, responding directly to concerns about being overheard.
new: Chats happen by text, not voice or video, so users don’t have to say anything sensitive out loud. Each chat has a set length and can end early, which leaves users in control of when and how much they share.
tactic: cs-t48 The rationale recital, with cs-t45 Erudite vernacular
why: The second sentence ends on an -ing tail that repeats the first sentence’s reason (not being overheard). Bounded chat format is jargon for what the reader already met in Scheduling: a set length that can end early. The new body gives one reason per sentence and ends on control, the new point.
src: Scheduling body (by text, 30 minutes, can end early). Interview insight 2. CONFIRMED on the page.

cur: Intro chats are text based only. Built for a time the user can be alone.
new: Intro chats happen by text, at a time the user can be alone.
why: The second half is a fragment. One sentence carries both facts.
src: No new claim.
